---
title: "Riverine flood-control ecosystem service"
format: html
---

## Purpose

Vegetated landscapes intercept rainfall, slow its passage into rivers and store part of it in
the soil. Where they do so upstream of towns and farmland, floods downstream are shallower than
they would otherwise be, and the damage those floods cause is smaller. That reduction in damage
is what this account values.

The scope is river flooding only. Coastal flooding, storm surge and pluvial flooding lie outside
it, following the hazard product the account uses. Coverage is 250 countries at 537 m, reported
in USD 2019.

## Method

Valuing this service requires answering a question that cannot be observed: how much flood damage
would occur if landscapes stopped absorbing rain. The account simulates a counterfactual world in
which ecosystems no longer retain water, routes the same storms through it, and takes the
difference.

Everything turns on one number per location, the **depth amplification**: the ratio of flood depth
in the degraded world to flood depth in the current one. Hydrology has no standard name for it,
because it has not previously been needed -- it exists here only because there is a paired
counterfactual world to run.

### Step 1, how absorbent each piece of land is

A curve number between 30 and 100 is assigned to every cell by crossing land cover with soil
hydrologic group, from USDA field measurements:

$$S = 25400 / \text{CN} - 254$$

$S$ is the potential maximum retention in millimetres. Forest on loam holds 208 mm; the same soil
stripped bare holds 41 mm. This is the only point in the account where vegetation enters the
physics.

### Step 2, how much extra water runs off

$$I_a = 0.2S, \qquad Q = (P - I_a)^2 / (P - I_a + S) \text{ for } P > I_a$$

The relation saturates. As $P$ grows large relative to $S$, runoff approaches total rainfall
regardless of land cover, so the service is concentrated in frequent events and the largest
proportional effects appear where storms are small relative to what the soil can hold.

### Step 3, following the water downhill

$$\text{ratio}(i) = \text{accum}(Q_\text{degraded})(i) / \text{accum}(Q_\text{current})(i)$$

Routing uses MERIT Hydro. On the Upper Mississippi, seven per cent more runoff at the point of
rainfall becomes twenty-two per cent more discharge in the river: routing roughly triples the
local effect, and that is what makes flood regulation a landscape service rather than a local one.

### Step 4, turning more water into deeper water

$$A(i) = [\text{ratio}(i)]^{f}, \qquad f \approx 0.4$$

At-a-station hydraulic geometry gives the split between width, depth and velocity. So 21.5% more
discharge produces 8% more depth. The exponent is the least constrained element of the chain and
is swept over 0.3 to 0.5.

## Two counterfactuals

**Bare soil** removes land cover entirely, setting curve numbers to the fallow values of the
reference tables. This is the world a gross product asks about, and it is the reference the
erosion account uses, so the two services are measured against one hypothetical landscape and can
be summed.

**In-situ degradation** raises curve numbers less: soils compacted and canopy thinned, the land
still present. Closer to what realistic degradation would produce, and reported alongside rather
than as a sensitivity.

Bare soil exceeds in-situ by about 2.5, and that ratio is stable to within four per cent across
both hazard products and both treatments of permanent water.

## Lambda

Lambda is 1 for this service. The counterfactual already isolates the ecosystem contribution: it
is a difference between two worlds identical in every respect except the ecosystem, so whatever
remains in the difference is the ecosystem's doing by construction.

The **prevention share** reported throughout is a different quantity and not an attribution
coefficient:

$$\text{prevention share} = (\text{EAD}_\text{degraded} - \text{EAD}_\text{current}) / \text{EAD}_\text{degraded}$$

An attribution share near 1 and a prevention share near 0.01 are not two estimates of one thing.

## Sign conventions

GEP is positive: it is damage that does not occur. Degradation raises expected annual damage, so
the difference is non-negative by construction and a negative value indicates a routing or
alignment fault rather than a result.

## Compute

The amplification field is built from rainfall and flow direction rather than from the hazard
maps, so it survives a change of hazard product. Building it is two weeks of single-threaded flow
accumulation over 75 billion cells; everything downstream of it is hours. `RUN.md` documents both
paths.
